transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-11-30 15:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Samira Gupta (Redwood SE), Luis Romero (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Head of Search, Atlas), Ben Lowe (Infra), Marta Silva (ML), Evan Cho (CTO)

Summary (auto):
Initial discovery for a similarity/rerank pilot. Customer currently evaluating hybrid search (BM25 + ANN) and a separate neural reranker. They want benchmarks for throughput and recall with different embedding dims, and want to understand tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for data residency and throughput SLOs. Security questions around SOC2, KMS, and audit logs were raised. Next steps: share pricing/security docs, exchange sample corpus, schedule benchmark session.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on this. Quick intros, then Samira and Luis will run through the tech questions.
[00:08] Priya: Hi, Priya here. We run search and retrieval for Atlas Research's knowledge graph and internal docs. Looking to improve semantic recall and also keep latency under, like, sub-200ms p95 for user queries.
[00:18] Ben: Ben, infra. We're responsible for the vector index and the service side. Current stack is Elastic for BM25 + a Faiss-based offline index.
[00:25] Marta: Marta, ML. I own embedding pipelines and reranker models.
[00:29] Samira: Great. To start, can you tell us current QPS and typical doc sizes? Helps us size batching and caching.
[00:35] Priya: Sure, cold numbers — average QPS is 60 during peak internal usage, but for public-facing search it can spike to 300 sustained for short windows. Documents are short to medium, 200–1,200 tokens, lots of metadata.
[00:46] Luis: Got it. And what's your current embedding dim?
[00:49] Marta: We're 768 dim using an off-the-shelf model right now, float32 during training then stored as float16. Concerned about index size and retrieval latency.
[00:58] Samira: Makes sense. On our side, typical tradeoffs we see: 128–256 dims can dramatically cut index size and ANN latency but may drop fine-grained recall for highly specialized corpora. 512–768 is common for high recall. Have you tried PCA/quantization?
[01:12] Marta: Not production-level PCA. We've done OPQ in Faiss experiments and 8-bit quantization. It saved space but added complexity to scoring.
[01:21] Jordan: Quick question — are you open to a hybrid approach? Many customers keep a smaller-dim embedding for ANN retrieval and then run a dedicated reranker model for final scoring. That reduces token usage on model calls.
[01:32] Priya: Yes, that's what we're leaning to. Our reranker is a T5-based model right now and that's expensive. We want to limit reranker invocations to top-k from ANN.
[01:41] Ben: Also — data residency. Some datasets must stay in EU cloud. That pushes us toward either Redwood Private or a Dedicated cluster in eu-west.
[01:49] Luis: When you say Private, do you mean on-prem or VPC-hosted?
[01:52] Ben: Prefer VPC-hosted for operations. On-prem for a few regulated clients but we'd prefer not to manage hardware.
[01:58] Samira: Good clarity. Redwood Dedicated can provision a capacity pool in eu-west with customer network peering and VPC options; Private is available for full control if required. For the pilot we often recommend Dedicated so we can run controlled benchmarks first.
[02:10] Marta: On throughput — what's realistic token throughput for a dedicated GPU cluster for reranking? Our reranker is T5-large style, inputs avg 768 tokens per doc pair.
[02:20] Luis: Also, how does Redwood handle continuous batching and KV cache when doing many short requests? Our traffic is bursty.
[02:26] Samira: For dedicated pools we can tune batching parameters — adaptive batch windows and prefilling KV caches for long conversational contexts. For rerank workloads we usually recommend batching candidate fights in a single call where possible; that is, pass batch of K pairs to the ranker in one request to amortize overhead. On T5-large equivalents we often see 20–40 reqs/sec per GPU depending on batch packing, quantization to int8/fp16, and sequence length. If you quantize and use kernel optimizations, numbers rise.
[02:51] Priya: And for ANN search, we currently use Faiss HNSW; we need sub-50ms retrieval for top-100 at 100 QPS. Is that achievable with Redwood-managed vectors or do we still need our own vector DB?
[03:03] Samira: Redwood can integrate with existing vector DBs (we've integrated with Faiss, Milvus, Pinecone, Weaviate) — we also offer a managed ANN service for hosted customers. Sub-50ms at 100 QPS for top-100 is borderline but doable with appropriate sharding, memory sizing, and using approximate indexes tuned for latency. If you're open to top-20 retrieval with rerank to expand recall, that reduces pressure.
[03:26] Ben: Our current indices are sharded by tenant, and we've seen CPU memory pressure during reindex jobs. How do you handle reindex/update windows?
[03:34] Luis: Also curious about consistency and eventual index updates — we have frequent small updates.
[03:39] Samira: For Dedicated we recommend background indexing workers with warmup nodes, rolling merges, and staged swaps. For Hosted we have a managed ingest path with incremental indexing; Private deployments can use local connectors. For frequent small updates, vector caches and prefix caches can reduce re-query overhead. We can share a best-practices doc for low-latency incremental indexing.
[03:57] Marta: Regarding dimensionality: you said 128–256 dims reduce size — but how do we quantify recall loss? Any tools you recommend?
[04:04] Samira: We typically run an embedding ablation — generate 128/256/512 for a sample query set and compute recall@K and MRR. Redwood's Optimize tooling can suggest quantization and batching profiles and will surface expected token cost and recall delta. We can run that on your 10k doc set.
[04:21] Jordan: Another consideration is model offload. Some customers prefer to offload embedding generation to edge microservices and only send embeddings to Redwood; others want Redwood to host model generation. Which approach are you leaning to?
[04:32] Priya: For now we want Redwood to host embeddings to reduce our ops burden, but for PII-sensitive docs we may generate locally.
[04:38] Evan: Security question — what's the KMS story? We need customer-managed keys and full audit logs for all model requests and stored embeddings.
[04:45] Samira: Dedicated and Private support customer KMS/HSM. We provide structured audit logs and can integrate with your SIEM. Hosted can also be configured with BYOK for certain enterprise plans. We'll share SOC2 and the KMS integration guide.
[04:58] Ben: About pricing — we need clarity on per-embedding cost vs per-token reranking cost, and how reserved capacity affects unit economics.
[05:05] Jordan: We'll send a detailed pricing sheet. Quick rule-of-thumb: dedicated reserved pools reduce per-token compute cost by ~30–50% versus hosted on-demand for heavy rerank workloads because you amortize the GPU.
[05:16] Marta: For the reranker, what's the preferred pattern — do you recommend running scorer in Redwood or as a sidecar service? Latency and cost both matter.
[05:24] Samira: If you need strict p95 SLOs, Dedicated with pinned GPUs and autoscaling bursts is better — less noisy neighbors. Sidecar services give you more control but bring operational overhead. For the pilot, run on Dedicated so we can benchmark realistic p95s; then you can decide on long-term placement.
[05:39] Priya: Can you walk through a typical pilot timeline and what success looks like?
[05:43] Jordan: Pilot usually 4–6 weeks: week 0 onboarding + security review, week 1 ingest sample corpus and baseline metrics, week 2 run embedding variants and ANN configs, week 3 reranker integration and combined end-to-end latency/recall benchmarks, week 4 analysis and decision. Success criteria we typically agree on: recall lift over baseline at fixed p95 latency, cost per query targets, and operational checklist (audit logs, KMS, SSO).
[06:05] Ben: For benchmarks we'll want reproducible scripts and access logs.
[06:08] Luis: Also, can you provide a sample of the telemetry we get from Redwood Console? Token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency, and traces are critical for our SREs.
[06:16] Samira: Absolutely — Redwood Console exposes per-request token counts, model breakdown, route dashboards, and exportable traces. We'll include screenshots and an exported example in the docs.
[06:26] Marta: One more technical nit — when doing hybrid search (BM25 + ANN), do you recommend scoring fusion server-side or client-side? We worry about normalization across score spaces.
[06:36] Samira: We recommend server-side fusion in the retrieval service to ensure consistent normalization and to avoid double round-trips. Many teams do BM25 to prune, ANN to expand, then a learned ranker. We can demo a fusion strategy in the benchmark.
[06:49] Priya: Ok, sounds good. What are immediate deliverables from Redwood after this call?
[06:53] Jordan: We'll send: 1) hosted vs dedicated pricing + pilot contract template; 2) security whitepaper + SOC2 link and KMS integration guide; 3) recommended embedding dim/quantization doc from Samira; 4) benchmark plan and required sample dataset spec.
[07:08] Evan: We'll circulate internal stakeholders and push the sample corpus. Aim to have the corpus and shard metadata to you by 2025-12-04.
[07:15] Jordan: Perfect. Anything else?
[07:18] Ben: One ask — can you include rough cost estimates for top-k rerank rates? Eg 1k QPS vs 100 QPS to show scaling?
[07:26] Jordan: Yes, we'll include example unit economics in the pricing doc.
[07:30] Priya: Great. Thanks, everyone.
[07:33] Jordan: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the artifacts and set the benchmark slot for week of 2025-12-08.
[07:39] Meeting end.
